newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - March 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - March 20.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for Reuters by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Times Of India
BHARATIYA JANATA PARTY, BAHUJAN SAMAJ PARTY TIE UP

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) formed a novel coalition government in Uttar Pradesh to end a political stalemate in the state. Under the arrangement, the chief ministership of the state would rotate every six months between the coalition partners. At the end of the year, the two parties would review the situation. In the 425-member assembly, the BJP has a strength of 177 while the BSP has 67 members. This was the first instance in the country's history, that such an arrangement was worked out between coalition partners.
The Economic Times
UNION BANK CUTS PLR TO 14 PCT

The Union Bank of India (UBI) announced a 50-basis-point cut in its prime lending rate, taking its rate for prime customers from 14.5 percent to 14 percent with effect from April 1. The 0.5 percentage point cut also brought down the maximum rate that could be charged by the bank to 18 percent from 18.5 percent. UBI was the first bank to respond to the finance minister's statement to cut lending rates.
Financial Express
STAMP DUTY CUT CLEARS HIND LEVER-BROOKE BOND MERGER

The Maharashtra government's decision to cut a stamp duty paved the way for the long-pending merger between Hindustan Lever (HLL) and Brooke Bond Lipton India (BBLIL). The HLL-BBLIL amalgamation was announced before January 1, 1996 but was put on hold due to what the company said was the deterrent stamp duty fees in the state. Under the new rates, the state finance minister proposed to levy a stamp duty of seven percent of the value of property or 0.7 percent of the value of shares issued, whichever was higher in case of amalgamations and mergers of companies.
ALL NEGOTIATED DEALS MUST END IN DELIVERY

Bourse regulator SEBI made it compulsory for all negotiated deals at the stock exchanges to end in delivery. To be effective from June 1, 1997, the move may severely curb illegal badla (forward) trade as well as the kerb market. The decision followed a meeting held by SEBI officials with the heads of all bourses after recent inspections of bourses revealed transactions made outside the exchanges, often entered the official channel as negotiated deals.
106 POINT INDEX CRASH NULLIFIES POST-BUDGET GAINS

The Bombay bourse slumped by 106.1 points to close at 3,690.39 points following heavy selling on major counters. The fall marked the total erosion of gains registered by the index since the budget was announced. The National bourse (NSE) echoed similar sentiments, with the NSE-50 index falling by 12.3 points to close at 1,052.05 points.
THREE PCT FISCAL DEFICIT BY 2000: FINANCE MINISTER

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said the country would achieve a GDP growth rate of eight percent by the turn of the century. He was also confident of the fiscal deficit being narrowed down to three percent. He, however, conceded that industry still faced a resource-crunch and steps were needed to bring down the interest rate.
GLOBAL COMMODITY EXCHANGE HANGS FIRE

The proposed global commodity exchange at Cochin, in Kerala, was facing teething problems. The article of association and memorandum of association of the Indian Pepper and Spices Trade Association-international commodity division, were earlier approved by the government. Guidelines for participation of foreign players were issued with the Finance Ministry's approval. But the ministry's delay in finalising the required formalities for repatriation of profits of foreign players was blocking the process.
Business Standard
NO FAVOURS TO PROMOTERS IN PORTFOLIO SELLOFF

The Finance Ministry ruled out the possibility of pressing financial institutions (FIs) to offload their portfolio of shares in favour of promoters. Various chambers were pressing the government with the demand ever since the bourse regulator ratified the new takeover code for companies. The term lending institutions had built up much of these portfolios over a period through forcible conversion of loan into equity. Finance Ministry officials said the matter would be decided by the FIs and the company.
FOREIGN FIRM'S ENTRY INTO DEFENCE RULED OUT

The involvement of multinationals in defence-related strategic areas was ruled out by the government. The minister of state for planning and science and technology said the report of the study team on strategic electronics for the ninth five year plan, had observed that there need not be any inhibition to involve multinationals in the strategic electronics sector provided they agreed to the transfer of critical technologies. He said the department of electronics had not suggested any modification in the general policy on foreign direct investment.
The Observer
FLEXIBLE INTEREST ON EXPORT CREDIT UNDER STUDY

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) planned to replace the fixed rate of interest on export credit with a system of flexible rates. This followed suggestions by bankers that such a measure would improve the offtake of export credit. Currently, the banks charge 13 percent interest on export. It was suggested that this be lowered by a couple of percentage points for borrowers with high creditworthiness, while those borrowers with low creditworthiness be charged the present rate, if not more.
CREDIT FACILITY FOR AIRBORNE TURBINE FUEL TO END FROM APRIL

Oil companies decided to stop the credit facility to all foreign airlines fuelling in India from April 1, 1997. Instead, the airlines were asked to deposit with the oil companies the amount equivalent to the value of the airlines' one month Airborne Turbine Fuel requirement. The amount was calculated on the basis of the airlines' average all-India upliftment for the previous three months, which would be reviewed quarterly and after a price revision.
MOODY'S UNLIKELY TO REVISE SOVERIGN RATING

Moody's Investor Services was unlikely to revise its sovereign rating of the Indian economy. Though the government marshalled all the facts and figures at its disposal before the Moody's representatives and Morgan Stanley came out strongly in favour of the former, the rating agency did not seem to be sufficiently convinced about the need to undertake further modification in its rating. Government sources said Moody's remained apprehensive about the revenue projections for fiscal 1997/98, while maintaining the budget had been over-optimistic about the private sector's ability to deliver the investment needs of key infrastructure sectors.
Business Line
BASMATI EXPORTS MAY ATTRACT EU DUTY

Indian basmati rice exports to the European Union (EU), currently duty-free, may attract a duty in excess of $300 per tonne following the approval of a new rice regulation by EU members. The CRS on brown long grain rice, which would replace the current reference price system (RPS), was voted by the EU's management committee. Exporters apprehended the introduction of the CRS virtually nullified the duty concession currently being accorded to Indian basmati rice.
